DiP-SD: Distributed Pipelined Speculative Decoding for Efficient LLM Inference at the Edge

Yaodan Xu, Sheng Zhou, Zhisheng Niu Affiliation: Department of Electronic Engineering, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100084, P.R. China Affiliation: xyd21@mails.tsinghua.edu.cn, {sheng.zhou, niuzhs}@tsinghua.edu.cn
Abstract

Speculative decoding has emerged as a promising technique for large language model (LLM) inference by accelerating autoregressive decoding via draft-then-verify. This paper studies a new edge scenario with multi-user inference, where draft tokens are generated locally on devices and subsequently offloaded to a centralized edge server for batch verification. The key challenge is to sustain high throughput under coupled decisions of (i) batching and pipeline scheduling and (ii) per-user draft token length. We propose DiP-SD, which exploits two complementary parallelism dimensions: device-level distributed drafting and phase-level draft–verify pipelining. We formulate a throughput-maximization objective, defined as the expected number of accepted tokens per unit time, and jointly optimize the number of batches, user-to-batch assignment, and integer draft lengths. To solve the resulting fractional mixed-integer program, DiP-SD scans the batch number and iteratively alternates between an association subproblem and a draft-length subproblem. Numerical results under a Qwen3-1.7B/Qwen3-32B device–edge deployment show that DiP-SD achieves up to 17.89×17.89\times throughput over autoregressive decoding (AD) and 1.93×1.93\times over AD with greedy batching.

I Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are now widely used in interactive applications such as assistants, search, coding copilots, and customer support. These services repeatedly invoke LLM inference to generate responses, making throughput and latency first-order system concerns. However, modern LLMs are parameter-heavy and resource-intensive, creating a fundamental tension between high inference cost and low-latency requirements for interactive use.

LLM inference is usually decomposed into a prefill stage and an autoregressive decode stage. While prefill can be amortized by caching and batching, decode remains latency-critical because tokens must be generated sequentially, making total latency proportional to output length. This token dependency makes decode the main throughput bottleneck for interactive services. Speculative decoding (SD) addresses this bottleneck by using a draft-then-verify scheme: a fast draft model proposes multiple draft tokens, and a stronger target model verifies them in parallel. Foundational SD work has shown that carefully designed accept/reject-and-resample procedures can preserve the target distribution while generating multiple tokens per target model call [1, 2, 3].

Recent SD research improves acceleration from several directions. One line improves draft-target alignment and acceptance through distillation or online adaptation [4, 5]. Another line redesigns the draft and verification structure, e.g., feature-space drafting, dynamic draft trees, or multi-head or self-speculative variants [6, 7, 8, 9]. As SD moves to distributed deployment, communication and synchronization become dominant concerns, including adaptive window control, selective feedback, and bandwidth-aware sparsification [10, 11, 12, 13].

Deploying inference at the edge can further improve responsiveness by placing models closer to users and reducing end-to-end delay. SD has also been explored in edge-oriented systems with heterogeneous devices and networks [14, 15, 16, 17, 18], but a key caveat is that SD does not automatically scale to multi-user, high-concurrency workloads: throughput can degrade when verification becomes a shared bottleneck[19, 15]. This makes batching unavoidable, where batching means grouping multiple inputs to the same model to be processed together so that compute and overhead can be amortized to increase throughput; however, existing edge SD systems typically adopt simple batching policies, e.g., static batching in SLED [14] or heuristic batch-size decisions in SPIN [15]. Beyond batching, pipeline parallelism has been studied to reduce bubbles and improve utilization: the authors of [20] pipeline draft and target phases via micro-batches within each draft–verify round, while FlowSpec [17] and PEARL [21] pipeline draft and target execution within a single request.

In this paper, we focus on a distributed edge setting where draft generation runs on multiple user-side devices locally and verification runs on an edge server, as shown in Fig. 1. This setting is increasingly practical because small LLMs have been deployed on end devices (e.g., tablets and smartphones), enabling local drafting with server-side verification. It creates two coupled parallelism dimensions: device-level distributed draft parallelism and phase-level draft–target pipeline parallelism. Unlike [20], which pipelines micro-batches within each draft–verify round, we pipeline across multiple batches over successive rounds, combining distributed drafting with batch-level verification pipelining.

DiP-SD is the first SD scheme to exploit batch-level pipeline parallelism between distributed drafting and centralized verification, with co-optimized speculation length and batching. The key control variables are the user-to-batch assignment, per-user speculative length, and the number of batches, which are tightly coupled by latency, memory, and communication constraints. Although DiP-SD is motivated by edge inference, it also applies to other SD deployments with distributed drafting and shared verification.

To address this coupled optimization problem, we propose a joint optimization framework. For each candidate number of batches, we iteratively alternate between a batch association subproblem and a draft-length subproblem, and select the best solution over scanned batch counts. Extensive numerical experiments show that the proposed scheme exhibits superior performance across all test points.

II System Model and Problem Formulation

II-A Edge Deployment Scenario

We consider an edge inference system serving MM user requests, indexed by ℳ={1,…,M}\mathcal{M}=\{1,\ldots,M\}. The system adopts a distributed speculative decoding framework: lightweight draft models are deployed on distributed edge devices, while a large-scale target model (the verifier) resides on a centralized edge server. As illustrated in Fig. 1, the draft and verification phases are decoupled across heterogeneous compute resources. This architecture naturally enables device-level parallelism during drafting and phase-level pipelining between the devices and the server. Specifically, in each speculation round, each device sequentially generates a sequence of draft tokens, which are subsequently transmitted to the edge server for concurrent batch verification. The target model processes these tokens in a single forward pass, and employs techniques such as rejection sampling to determine their validity.

The iterative speculation process for each request follows a four-stage cycle:

  1. 1.

    Local Drafting: Each edge device independently employs its lightweight draft model to generate a sequence of tokens in a serial manner. These draft tokens are subsequently offloaded to the edge server.

  2. 2.

    Batch Verification: The edge server validates the received draft tokens through the target model in a single forward pass. It identifies the first mismatched token for each request, discards all subsequent incorrect predictions, and simultaneously produces one bonus token following the last accepted position, ensuring at least one token is generated per round. In our system, multiple requests are grouped into batches and verified together to amortize the overhead of target model inference.

  3. 3.

    Synchronization: The server transmits the verified tokens and the bonus token back to the respective device, ensuring both sides are synchronized with the latest generation state.

  4. 4.

    State Update: The device updates its local KV cache and resumes the next drafting round, starting from the newly received bonus token.

For the optimization, we introduce a batch count NN with index set 𝒩={1,…,N}\mathcal{N}=\{1,\ldots,N\}, where N∈{2,…,M}N\in\{2,\ldots,M\}. We use “batch” to denote a set of requests verified together at the edge server. Verification proceeds in NN pipeline stages, where stage nn verifies batch nn (thus nn also indicates the verification order/slot). Fig. 2 illustrates one example.

Request mm has prefix length imi_{m}, communication overhead τmc\tau_{m}^{\mathrm{c}}, and acceptance parameter αm\alpha_{m}. Here τmc\tau_{m}^{\mathrm{c}} is the per-round communication latency between the device and the edge server. The communication link can be wireless or wired, and the SD payload only contains drafted tokens and (when needed by the verification protocol) a small amount of probability information (e.g., draft token log-probabilities and sparse target logits), so the transmitted volume is small and we consider τmc\tau_{m}^{\mathrm{c}} as a constant. The prefix length imi_{m} counts both the original input prompt and the previously accepted tokens (i.e., the current context length at the beginning of the optimization window).

We focus on optimizing the speculative decoding (decode) process and omit prefill latency, since prefill is executed once per request and can be treated as an additive constant. Since each request spans hundreds of tokens and thus many SD rounds, the set of active requests and system parameters are approximately stationary within each optimization horizon. Although the prefix length imi_{m} grows by the number of accepted tokens each round, this increment is small relative to the full generation length, so we treat imi_{m} as a constant.

II-B Speculative Decoding Utility Model

Each user mm selects integer draft length lm∈ℕ+l_{m}\in\mathbb{N}_{+}. The token acceptance rate αm∈(0,1)\alpha_{m}\in(0,1) characterizes the statistical alignment between the draft and target models. Given that this rate inherently fluctuates across different tasks, we model the acceptance rate as a user-specific parameter to account for such heterogeneity. The expected number of accepted tokens of one speculative round for user mm is

um​(lm)=1−αmlm+11−αm,\displaystyle u_{m}(l_{m})=\frac{1-\alpha_{m}^{l_{m}+1}}{1-\alpha_{m}}, (1)

where each draft token is accepted independently with probability αm\alpha_{m} (geometric acceptance model [1]), and one bonus token is always generated regardless of acceptance outcomes. The total expected accepted tokens across all users is

U⁡(𝐥)=∑m=1Mum​(lm).\displaystyle U(\mathbf{l})=\sum_{m=1}^{M}u_{m}(l_{m}). (2)

II-C Transformer-Cost Primitives

Let Ξ∈{d,v}\Xi\in\{\mathrm{d},\mathrm{v}\} denote draft and verification (target) models. Model Ξ\Xi has JΞJ_{\Xi} decoder blocks, hidden dimension h1Ξh_{1}^{\Xi}, and hidden dimension h2Ξh_{2}^{\Xi} in feed-forward network (FFN).

Following standard decoder-only cost scaling, we define

Fd​(i)\displaystyle F^{\mathrm{d}}(i) =4​Jd​h1d​(2​h1d+i+1+h2d),\displaystyle=4J_{\mathrm{d}}h_{1}^{\mathrm{d}}\!\left(2h_{1}^{\mathrm{d}}+i+1+h_{2}^{\mathrm{d}}\right), (3)
Fv​(L,I)\displaystyle F^{\mathrm{v}}(L,I) =4​Jv​h1v​L​(2​h1v+I+L+h2v).\displaystyle=4J_{\mathrm{v}}h_{1}^{\mathrm{v}}L\!\left(2h_{1}^{\mathrm{v}}+I+L+h_{2}^{\mathrm{v}}\right). (4)

Intuitively, Fd​(⋅)F^{\mathrm{d}}(\cdot) and Fv​(⋅,⋅)F^{\mathrm{v}}(\cdot,\cdot) capture the compute intensity of draft and verification for one round, growing with the context length ii and the batch-wise maximum draft length and prefix length (L,I)(L,I). Following [20], we model the per-step drafting and verification latency as affine functions of the product b​FbF:

Gm​(b,F)\displaystyle G_{m}(b,F) =cm​b​F+βm,\displaystyle=c_{m}bF+\beta_{m}, (5)
Gv​(b,F)\displaystyle G^{\mathrm{v}}(b,F) =cv​b​F+βv.\displaystyle=c^{\mathrm{v}}bF+\beta^{\mathrm{v}}. (6)

The functions Gm​(⋅,⋅)G_{m}(\cdot,\cdot) and Gv​(⋅,⋅)G^{\mathrm{v}}(\cdot,\cdot) characterize the latency for drafting and verification, respectively. Parameters (c,β)(c,\beta) are obtained from profiling and capture per-compute scaling and fixed overhead, and bb is the batch size. This affine dependence on batch size is consistent with empirical observations reported in [22, 23].

II-D Assignment and Batch-Aggregation Constraints

Binary assignment and one-batch-per-user constraints are

xm​n∈{0,1},∀m,n,\displaystyle x_{mn}\in\{0,1\},\quad\forall m,n, (7)
∑n=1Nxm​n=1,∀m.\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{N}x_{mn}=1,\quad\forall m. (8)

Here xm​nx_{mn} indicates whether user mm is associated with batch nn (and thus verified in stage nn). Draft lengths are positive integers:

lm∈ℕ+,∀m.\displaystyle l_{m}\in\mathbb{N}_{+},\quad\forall m. (9)

Batch size is

bn=∑m=1Mxm​n,bn≥1,∀n.\displaystyle b_{n}=\sum_{m=1}^{M}x_{mn},\quad b_{n}\geq 1,\quad\forall n. (10)

The condition bn≥1b_{n}\geq 1 enforces valid fixed-NN batching, i.e., each declared batch is active.

Batch-level max variables are represented by epigraph inequalities:

Ln≥lm​xm​n,∀m,n,\displaystyle L_{n}\geq l_{m}x_{mn},\quad\forall m,n, (11)
In≥im​xm​n,∀m,n.\displaystyle I_{n}\geq i_{m}x_{mn},\quad\forall m,n. (12)

Thus, (Ln,In)(L_{n},I_{n}) act as batch-wise maxima of speculative length and prefix length.

II-E Latency-Coupling Constraints

The per-user drafting latency is defined as:

τmd=lm​Gm​(1,Fd​(im)),∀m.\displaystyle\tau_{m}^{\mathrm{d}}=l_{m}G_{m}\left(1,F^{\mathrm{d}}(i_{m})\right),\quad\forall m. (13)

This formulation reflects that the drafting phase is executed locally on each device without batching. Specifically, as the drafting process is inherently serial, the total latency is calculated as the product of the draft length lml_{m} and the per-token drafting time.

Batch draft time uses max-epigraph constraints:

tnd≥xm​n​(τmd+τmc),∀m,n.\displaystyle t_{n}^{\mathrm{d}}\geq x_{mn}\!\left(\tau_{m}^{\mathrm{d}}+\tau_{m}^{\mathrm{c}}\right),\quad\forall m,n. (14)

so tndt_{n}^{\mathrm{d}} captures when all requests in batch nn have completed drafting and communication.

Batch verification latency is

tnv=Gv​(bn,Fv​(Ln,In)),∀n.\displaystyle t_{n}^{\mathrm{v}}=G^{\mathrm{v}}\!\left(b_{n},F^{\mathrm{v}}(L_{n},I_{n})\right),\quad\forall n. (15)

which depends on the batch size bnb_{n} and the batch-wise maxima (Ln,In)(L_{n},I_{n}) due to padding. Stage duration must cover verification:

Tn≥tnv,∀n.\displaystyle T_{n}\geq t_{n}^{\mathrm{v}},\quad\forall n. (16)

Here TnT_{n} is the stage duration in the pipeline schedule: it can exceed tnvt_{n}^{\mathrm{v}} to satisfy global precedence constraints and account for pipeline bubbles.

The total pipeline span SS is the steady-state cycle time over which one complete SD round (all NN batches) is processed:

S=∑n=1NTn.\displaystyle S=\sum_{n=1}^{N}T_{n}. (17)

Pipeline precedence requires the pipeline span to cover both the draft completion time and the verification latency of batch nn:

S≥tnd+tnv,∀n.\displaystyle S\geq t_{n}^{\mathrm{d}}+t_{n}^{\mathrm{v}},\quad\forall n. (18)

II-F Memory Constraints at Edge Side

Since batching is not employed on the user side, we assume that the memory footprint of the draft model remains well within the device’s limits. Consequently, our analysis focuses on the memory constraints at the edge server, which performs batch processing for the target model inference. With FP16 precision, the model parameters occupy a memory footprint of approximately:

Γpv=Jv​(8​(h1v)2+4​h1v​h2v).\displaystyle\Gamma_{\mathrm{p}}^{\mathrm{v}}=J_{\mathrm{v}}\!\left(8(h_{1}^{\mathrm{v}})^{2}+4h_{1}^{\mathrm{v}}h_{2}^{\mathrm{v}}\right). (19)

KV-cache component for batch nn is:

Γkv,nv=4​Jv​h1v​bn​In,∀n.\displaystyle\Gamma_{\mathrm{kv},n}^{\mathrm{v}}=4J_{\mathrm{v}}h_{1}^{\mathrm{v}}b_{n}I_{n},\quad\forall n. (20)

The memory feasibility constraint is then:

Γpv+Γkv,nv≤Γmaxv,∀n.\displaystyle\Gamma_{\mathrm{p}}^{\mathrm{v}}+\Gamma_{\mathrm{kv},n}^{\mathrm{v}}\leq\Gamma_{\max}^{\mathrm{v}},\quad\forall n. (21)

II-G Overall Joint Optimization Objective

We define the throughput RR as the expected number of accepted tokens per unit time:

R≜U⁡(𝐥)S,\displaystyle R\triangleq\frac{U(\mathbf{l})}{S}, (22)

where U⁡(𝐥)U(\mathbf{l}) is defined in (2) and SS is the total pipeline span in (17). This formulation is valid under the stationary workload assumption: since the pipeline schedule repeats across successive SD rounds within each optimization period, it suffices to evaluate throughput over a single representative round.

The final design jointly optimizes assignment 𝐱\mathbf{x}, speculative lengths 𝐥\mathbf{l}, batch count NN, and other auxiliary variables:

𝒫:max𝐱,𝐥,N,aux\displaystyle\mathcal{P}:\quad\max_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{l},N,\mathrm{aux}}\; R\displaystyle R (23)
s.t.  (7)–(21),\displaystyle\eqref{eq:C_x_binary}\text{--}\eqref{eq:C_mem_total},
N∈{2,…,M}.\displaystyle N\in\{2,\ldots,M\}. (24)

III Proposed Joint Solver

III-A Joint Solver Overview

The joint design problem is challenging because it involves (i) integer decisions (user association and draft length) and (ii) a throughput objective that is fractional in the total latency. We solve it with a two-level joint solver. At the outer level, we scan the number of batches N∈{2,…,M}N\in\{2,\ldots,M\}. For each fixed NN, we solve

𝒫(N):max𝐱,𝐥,aux\displaystyle\mathcal{P}(N):\quad\max_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{l},\mathrm{aux}}\; R⁡(N)\displaystyle R(N) (25)
s.t.  (7)–(21).\displaystyle\eqref{eq:C_x_binary}\text{--}\eqref{eq:C_mem_total}.

where R⁡(N)R(N) is the throughput defined in (22) under fixed NN. To handle the coupling between user-to-batch association and integer draft lengths, we apply alternating optimization:

𝐱(r+1)\displaystyle\mathbf{x}^{(r+1)} ←arg⁡min⁡S⁡(N,𝐥(r)),\displaystyle\leftarrow\arg\min S(N,\mathbf{l}^{(r)}), (26)
𝐥(r+1)\displaystyle\mathbf{l}^{(r+1)} ←arg⁡max⁡R⁡(N,𝐱(r+1)).\displaystyle\leftarrow\arg\max R(N,\mathbf{x}^{(r+1)}). (27)

The outer loop stops when 𝐥\mathbf{l} is unchanged and the throughput change is below tolerance. Finally, we select the best solution over the scanned batch counts. The overall workflow is summarized in Algorithm 1. Each subproblem reduces to a mixed-integer linear program (MILP) that we solve using SCIP through its Python interface PySCIPOpt [24, 25].

In implementation, we additionally impose practical variable bounds to tighten the MILPs and improve numerical stability. In particular, we use the bound parameters (Lub,Iub,Tub,Sub)(L_{\mathrm{ub}},I_{\mathrm{ub}},T_{\mathrm{ub}},S_{\mathrm{ub}}) as upper bounds for draft lengths, prefix lengths, and auxiliary timing variables.

III-B 𝐱\mathbf{x}-Subproblem

Given fixed 𝐥\mathbf{l}, we solve

𝒳(N,𝐥):min𝐱,𝐓,aux\displaystyle\mathcal{X}(N,\mathbf{l}):\quad\min_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{T},\mathrm{aux}}\; S\displaystyle S\quad (28)
s.t.   (7)–(8),(10)–(12),\displaystyle\eqref{eq:C_x_binary}\text{--}\eqref{eq:C_x_assign},\eqref{eq:C_b_def}\text{--}\eqref{eq:C_I_epi},
(14)–(21).\displaystyle\eqref{eq:C_td}\text{--}\eqref{eq:C_mem_total}.

This step decides batching assignment and batch-wise timing variables under full feasibility constraints.

III-C 𝐥\mathbf{l}-Subproblem: Binary Reformulation + Dinkelbach

Given fixed 𝐱\mathbf{x}, we solve

ℒ(N,𝐱):max𝐥\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(N,\mathbf{x}):\quad\max_{\mathbf{l}}\; U⁡(𝐥)S⁡(𝐥∣𝐱)\displaystyle\frac{U(\mathbf{l})}{S(\mathbf{l}\mid\mathbf{x})} (29)
s.t.  (9),(11),(13)–(21).\displaystyle\eqref{eq:C_l_integer},\ \eqref{eq:C_L_epi},\ \eqref{eq:C_tau_d}\text{--}\eqref{eq:C_mem_total}.

We constrain the draft length to lm∈{1,…,Lub}l_{m}\in\{1,\ldots,L_{\mathrm{ub}}\}, where LubL_{\mathrm{ub}} denotes the upper bound. This constraint is justified by the diminishing returns of the utility function um​(lm)u_{m}(l_{m}) as lml_{m} increases. Furthermore, empirical evidence from prior speculative decoding studies [1, 2] suggests that the optimal draft length typically falls within the range of 5–15. To handle integer draft lengths efficiently, we use binary selectors:

ym​k∈{0,1},∑k=1Lubym​k=1,lm=∑k=1Lubk​ym​k,\displaystyle y_{mk}\in\{0,1\},\quad\sum_{k=1}^{L_{\mathrm{ub}}}y_{mk}=1,\quad l_{m}=\sum_{k=1}^{L_{\mathrm{ub}}}k\,y_{mk}, (30)
zn​k∈{0,1},∑k=0Lubzn​k=1,Ln=∑k=0Lubk​zn​k.\displaystyle z_{nk}\in\{0,1\},\quad\sum_{k=0}^{L_{\mathrm{ub}}}z_{nk}=1,\quad L_{n}=\sum_{k=0}^{L_{\mathrm{ub}}}k\,z_{nk}. (31)

For users in batch nn, max-consistency is enforced by

Ln≥lm,∀m∈ℬn(𝐱),∀n,\displaystyle L_{n}\geq l_{m},\quad\forall m\in\mathcal{B}_{n}(\mathbf{x}),\ \forall n, (32)

where ℬn​(𝐱)\mathcal{B}_{n}(\mathbf{x}) denotes the user set of the nn-th batch.

Define lookup utility

um​k=1−αmk+11−αm,U⁡(𝐲)=∑m=1M∑k=1Lubum​k​ym​k.\displaystyle u_{mk}=\frac{1-\alpha_{m}^{k+1}}{1-\alpha_{m}},\quad U(\mathbf{y})=\sum_{m=1}^{M}\sum_{k=1}^{L_{\mathrm{ub}}}u_{mk}y_{mk}. (33)

We handle the fractional objective via the classic Dinkelbach method[26]. At Dinkelbach iteration tt, solve inner mixed-integer problem:

max𝐲,𝐳,aux\displaystyle\max_{\mathbf{y},\mathbf{z},\mathrm{aux}}\; U⁡(𝐲)−q(t)​S​(𝐲,𝐳)\displaystyle U(\mathbf{y})-q^{(t)}S(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{z}) (34)
s.t.  (13)–(21),(30)–(32).\displaystyle\eqref{eq:C_tau_d}\text{--}\eqref{eq:C_mem_total},\ \eqref{eq:y_def}\text{--}\eqref{eq:Lmax_cons}.

Then update

q(t+1)=U⁡(𝐲(t))S⁡(𝐲(t),𝐳(t)).\displaystyle q^{(t+1)}=\frac{U(\mathbf{y}^{(t)})}{S(\mathbf{y}^{(t)},\mathbf{z}^{(t)})}. (35)

Stop when

|U⁡(𝐲(t))−q(t)​S​(𝐲(t),𝐳(t))|≤ϵ,\displaystyle\left|U(\mathbf{y}^{(t)})-q^{(t)}S(\mathbf{y}^{(t)},\mathbf{z}^{(t)})\right|\leq\epsilon, (36)

or an equivalent throughput-change threshold is met. Each inner problem is a MILP. We solve these MILPs using SCIP/PySCIPOpt [24, 25].

III-D Batch-Count Selection and Final Deployment Decision

For each fixed NN, let the converged throughput be R⋆​(N)R^{\star}(N). Then we select

N⋆=arg⁡maxN∈{2,…,M}​R⋆​(N).\displaystyle N^{\star}=\arg\max_{N\in\{2,\ldots,M\}}R^{\star}(N). (37)

III-E Complexity Discussion

As shown in Algorithm 1, DiP-SD scans the batch count and alternates MILP-based 𝐱\mathbf{x} and 𝐥\mathbf{l} updates for each fixed NN to maximize throughput. Let IoutI_{\mathrm{out}} be the number of alternating iterations and IdinI_{\mathrm{din}} be Dinkelbach iterations. Per fixed NN, complexity is approximately

𝒪⁡(Iout​(𝒞𝐱​(M,N)+Idin​𝒞𝐥​(M,N,Lub))),\mathcal{O}\!\left(I_{\mathrm{out}}\big(\mathcal{C}_{\mathbf{x}}(M,N)+I_{\mathrm{din}}\mathcal{C}_{\mathbf{l}}(M,N,L_{\mathrm{ub}})\big)\right),

where 𝒞𝐱\mathcal{C}_{\mathbf{x}} and 𝒞𝐥\mathcal{C}_{\mathbf{l}} denote solver-dependent inner complexities. The outer batch-count scan multiplies this by the number of tested batch counts.

IV Numerical Results

IV-A System Setup

We evaluate DiP-SD using the Qwen3 model series[27]. Specifically, Qwen3-1.7B serves as the draft model on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090, and Qwen3-32B serves as the target model on an NVIDIA A100-80GB edge server. Their transformer dimensions, (Jd,h1d,h2d)(J_{\mathrm{d}},h_{1}^{\mathrm{d}},h_{2}^{\mathrm{d}}) and (Jv,h1v,h2v)(J_{\mathrm{v}},h_{1}^{\mathrm{v}},h_{2}^{\mathrm{v}}) respectively, along with all other default parameters, are listed in Table II. Latency parameters are obtained by profiling each model on its respective hardware and fitting the measurements to the affine latency model in (5)–(6). The default acceptance rate is estimated from inference statistics over 100 sampled prompts. All remaining experiments are conducted via numerical simulation under the default parameters in Table II. All latency parameters are in milliseconds (ms) and memory parameters are in bytes (B).

We compare five methods:

  • •

    DiP-SD (proposed): joint solver that scans batch counts and alternates 𝐱/𝐥\mathbf{x}/\mathbf{l} updates.

  • •

    AD: edge-only large model autoregressive decoding without speculative drafting. No batching scheme is applied.

  • •

    AD w/ greedy batching: AD with greedy memory-feasible batching: sort users by imi_{m} in descending order, then pack them into batches sequentially until the memory bound would be violated.

  • •

    DiP-SD w/o batching: enforce N=MN=M and one user per batch; optimize only 𝐥\mathbf{l}.

  • •

    DiP-SD w/ fixed lm=7l_{m}=7: fix lml_{m} and optimize only 𝐱\mathbf{x}.

The primary metric is throughput, which is expected accepted tokens per unit time in our context. Since SS is in ms, R=U⁡(𝐥)/SR=U(\mathbf{l})/S has unit token/ms, and we report throughput with 1000×R1000\times R token/s.

IV-B Results

IV-B1 Homogeneous Setting

We first consider a homogeneous-user setting, where all users share the same per-user parameters at each test point. We conduct two groups of experiments: 1) throughput versus user number MM (number of concurrent users), with M∈{2,4,…,14}M\in\{2,4,\ldots,14\}; and 2) throughput versus token acceptance rate αm\alpha_{m}, with M=6M=6, αm∈{0.70,0.75,0.80,0.85,0.90,0.95}\alpha_{m}\in\{0.70,0.75,0.80,0.85,0.90,0.95\}. Other parameters are set as the default values in Table II.

Fig. 3(a) shows that the proposed DiP-SD consistently achieves the highest throughput among all methods. The basic AD scheme, lacking batching, has throughput independent of user count. DiP-SD without batching exhibits throughput that first increases with MM and then plateaus. In contrast, batching-enabled methods — DiP-SD, DiP-SD with fixed lm=7l_{m}=7, and AD with greedy batching — all exhibit approximately linear throughput growth with increasing MM. This is because the throughput numerator scales proportionally with MM, while newly added users are absorbed into existing batches with negligible increase in total pipeline span SS. The performance gap between DiP-SD and AD with greedy batching widens as MM increases; at peak, DiP-SD achieves 1.38×1.38\times over AD with greedy batching and 17.89×17.89\times over AD. Meanwhile, DiP-SD with fixed lm=7l_{m}=7 underperforms DiP-SD, highlighting the importance of draft length selection. Furthermore, DiP-SD without batching is substantially outperformed by the three batching-enabled methods when M≥6M\geq 6, demonstrating the critical role of batching in supporting concurrent multi-user inference.

As illustrated in Fig. 3(b), the throughput of all SD-based benchmarks exhibits a monotonic increase with the acceptance rate αm\alpha_{m}. This is because a higher αm\alpha_{m} allows more drafted tokens accepted per round. In contrast, the throughput of AD baselines remains constant, as they do not leverage speculative execution. The proposed DiP-SD scheme maintains the highest throughput at all testpoints. Quantitatively, as αm\alpha_{m} increases from 0.700.70 to 0.950.95 (with M=6M=6), the throughput of DiP-SD grows from 74.1374.13 to 117.56117.56 token/s, representing a 1.59×1.59\times improvement. At its peak, the proposed DiP-SD achieves a substantial speedup of 11.25×11.25\times over the vanilla AD and 1.93×1.93\times over the AD baseline with greedy batching, demonstrating the superiority of our method in high-acceptance regimes. However, for model pairs with a large size gap, the acceptance rate is usually moderate. In our setting, the default αm\alpha_{m} is 0.780.78, at which DiP-SD achieves around 1.38×1.38\times throughput over AD with greedy batching. It is also noted that DiP-SD with fixed lm=7l_{m}=7 and DiP-SD without batching do not always outperform AD with greedy batching: their performance crossover points occur near αm=0.75\alpha_{m}=0.75 and αm=0.85\alpha_{m}=0.85, respectively, below which the overhead of failed drafting offsets the gains of speculation. This further confirms that adaptive draft length and batching each make an essential contribution to throughput improvement.

IV-B2 Heterogeneous Setting

We next evaluate three single-factor heterogeneous cases with fixted user number M=6M=6. Case 1 heterogenizes prefix length imi_{m} with values {200,320,440,560,680,800}\{200,320,440,560,680,800\}, while Case 2 considers non-uniform acceptance rates αm\alpha_{m} ranging from {0.80,0.82,0.84,0.86,0.88,0.90}\{0.80,0.82,0.84,0.86,0.88,0.90\}. In Case 3, we heterogenize the draft-side latency coefficients (cm,βm)(c_{m},\beta_{m}) by applying the scale set {0.2,0.5,1.0,3.0,5.0,7.0}\{0.2,0.5,1.0,3.0,5.0,7.0\} to the default values.

Fig. 4 shows that DiP-SD remains the best-performing method across all three heterogeneous cases, achieving up to 8.09×8.09\times throughput over AD and 1.39×1.39\times over AD with greedy batching. The proposed throughput ranges from 78.4978.49 to 84.5384.53 token/s across the three scenarios, with the αm\alpha_{m}-heterogeneous case yielding the largest advantage. This gain is primarily attributed to the inclusion of several users whose acceptance rates exceed the default value, which directly raises the expected number of accepted tokens per verification round. From an architectural perspective, variations in αm\alpha_{m} fundamentally affect the utility of speculation, whereas heterogeneity in prefix length or latency coefficients primarily impacts the latency components of the system. It is also worth noting that DiP-SD-based methods suffer a pronounced throughput degradation under heterogeneous (cm,βm)(c_{m},\beta_{m}): the imbalance across user-side latencies disrupts the pipeline, enlarging the total span and reducing pipeline efficiency.

V Conclusion

This paper presented DiP-SD, a joint optimization framework for distributed pipelined speculative decoding. We maximize throughput, defined as the expected number of accepted tokens per unit time, under latency, memory, and communication constraints. DiP-SD jointly optimizes user-to-batch association and integer draft lengths via an outer scan over the batch count and an alternating update between the two subproblems. Numerical results show that DiP-SD consistently achieves the highest throughput across all evaluated scenarios, with substantial gains over baselines.

DiP-SD targets edge-first deployments, where multiple devices host lightweight drafting and a nearby edge server performs shared verification. This makes the framework suitable for edge assistants, vehicle–road–edge collaborative inference, and other low-latency interactive LLM applications. Beyond edge serving, the framework also applies to general multi-accelerator deployments with distributed drafting and shared verification, covering both single-node and multi-node GPU configurations. Future work includes real-world deployment and online adaptation to nonstationary workloads.
